SEAM DECIDED, argued. ext/Playground is READ-ONLY to me and calls tree() AND .select(), so it cannot be updated inside my fence, and the brief's non-negotiable is that existing callers keep working. ui/ must never import ux/, so ui.tree cannot become a re-export of the class either. Therefore the split is ADDITIVE, not destructive: ui/tree/tree.js keeps tree() byte-compatible and keeps the .ui-tree-* css(); ux/Tree/Tree.js imports ui/tree/tree.js FOR THAT STYLESHEET (a ux imports a ui template, the blessed direction) and re-implements the stateful half as a class wearing the same classes. Cost: ~45 lines of closure live on in ui/ until ext/Playground moves. Rejected: (a) making tree() markup-only, which breaks Playground's rail; (b) a written proposal that leaves Playground broken until the owner applies it.

Naming census before the first class was written: classify() stamps a class for EVERY constructor in the chain, so Tree/TreeItem/TreeRow/TreeKeys/TreeKeysRow emit .tree .tree-item .tree-row .tree-keys .tree-keys-row. grep over public/ **/*.css + *.js found ONE near hit, ext/demo/exhibit.css:92 .tree-preview, which needs the exact token .tree-preview and cannot match any of ours. No collision. Added 'ux-tree-     ux/Tree' to styles/css-scopes.txt by exact-string edit (a sibling had just added ux-wizard- and another added ux-auth- while I worked; the anchored edit survived both).

KEYBOARD PROVED HEADLESS, ui-test drive.mjs, 20 steps, zero non-LiveReload console errors. Evidence per step: 12 rows and exactly ONE tabbable at every single step (the roving tabindex claim); click row 0 -> active 'ux', selected ['ux']; ArrowDown x2 -> active AND tabbable both 'Tree.js'; ArrowLeft on the leaf -> active 'Tree' (stepped OUT to parent); ArrowLeft on the open branch -> open list ['ux','Tree'] becomes ['ux'] and the tree box shrinks 133px; ArrowRight -> reopens, +133px; Enter -> selected ['Tree.js'] and the focused row's outlineColor reads rgb(255,143,96) = --prim, so Tree.css's one rule is live; End -> 'ui' (last visible); Home -> 'ux'.

ui-test trap, cost one run: drive.mjs's parse() splits args on whitespace, so a selector containing spaces MUST be quoted or page.click() receives only the first token. Second trap: a leaf demo page has TWO copies of its demo in the DOM -- the live one in .demo-stage and a zero-size one inside the PARENT page's Variants preview card -- so a bare .ux-tree-keys selector grabs the hidden card and every click times out. Scope every selector to .demo-stage.

Probed the orange ring around the whole rail in the proof shot before believing it was mine: it is ext/layout's inspector, .rail wearing layout-hot layout-selected because clicking inside a demo points the layout bar at that box. Pre-existing demo chrome, not Tree.css. The row's own ring is the second entry, 184x33, same --prim.

lesson: THE NAMED-PROGRESSION PATTERN HOLDS, and it is cheap. Tree -> TreeKeys is 100 lines including the key map, and it needed ZERO changes to Tree -- no hook added, no option, no callback threaded through. The reason is that Tree had already put every behavior in a method and every part on the constructor, so TreeKeys had somewhere to stand. The name also does real work: TreeKeys says what it IS, and classify() turns it into .tree-keys, which is the class the one CSS rule scopes to. A TreeDrag would land the same way. Verdict: name the subclass, never number it, never option it.

lesson: WHAT THE STATIC-PARTS PATTERN BOUGHT, concretely. TreeKeys sets exactly ONE static (TreeKeys.Row = class TreeKeysRow extends Tree.Row) and inherits Tree.Item untouched, because extends copies the static side. Tree.Row is unaffected, so a plain Tree still has zero tab stops -- the extension cannot leak into the base. Reaching parts through the LIVE class is what makes it work: Tree.item() says new this.constructor.Item and Item.row() says new this.tree.constructor.Row, so a TreeKeys builds TreeKeysRow with nothing wired. Hard-coding new Tree.Row() there would have made the extension impossible and the bug would have been invisible. Second, unplanned dividend: rows is a Map and items build depth-first, so [...rows.values()] IS DOM order -- TreeKeys walks the rows for arrow navigation and added NO state of its own for it.

lesson: WHAT THE GRADUATION COST. (1) One duplicated implementation, ~45 lines: tree() lives on in ui/ because ext/Playground calls it from outside the fence. Not design debt, fence debt -- a one-line import change closes it. (2) Three method names had to dodge View: Item.toggle -> flip, Row.text -> label, Row.toggle -> caret. Every method on a View subclass shadows the base silently, and text() in particular would have broken every .text() caller. Census the base class before naming a method. (3) One class field trap: View renders inside its constructor, so tag/classes/indent had to go on the PROTOTYPE -- a class field arrives after the first draw. (4) One new CSS rule total, and only because roving focus is a state the template cannot own. Everything else was free: both tiers read the same tokens, so ui-contrast ui-compact re-skins the class with no work at all (proved on /framework/ux/Tree/words/).

lesson: the ux/ tier needs a module-shape verdict from the owner. Every real module page under core/ ext/ dev/ is a new Doc({notes, files}), which is what makes /module/doc/x/ a browsable route. ux/Tree shipped as a plain Page like its sibling ui/tree, because Doc puts content() inside the Overview rail's intro card and that would have re-columned the bleed exhibit -- a layout change bigger than the deliverable. Consequence: ux/Tree/doc/decisions.md is linked as a raw .md, exactly as ui/tree/doc/decisions.md has always been. Converting ux/Tree to a Doc is a follow-up worth making once the tier settles, and it should be one call for all three ux modules, not three.
